GitHub OAuth App: setup and validated read-only test

Validated 2026-10-28. Result: token exchange HTTP 200; exactly one authenticated GET /user HTTP 200; granted scopes empty. This guide covers an OAuth App, rather than a GitHub App. GitHub recommends considering GitHub Apps for finer permissions and repository selection; this experiment deliberately tested the requested OAuth App route. Official comparison and setup.

The user starts already signed in to GitHub. Signing in does not eliminate later GitHub step-up verification.

1. Create the personal OAuth App

Open Settings → Developer settings → OAuth apps → New OAuth App. First-time accounts may see Register a new application. Use public-safe app metadata. Official registration steps.

For this local test, the host entered:

Field Tested value
Application name OAuth Guide validation [identifies this integration to users; in production, use your recognizable product name]
Homepage URL http://127.0.0.1:8765 [local test only; production example: https://your-agent.example/]
Description Private local OAuth setup validation. [optional summary users can see; describe what your integration does; leave blank if unnecessary and never include secrets or internal details]
Redirect URI http://127.0.0.1:8765/callback [local test only; production example: https://your-agent.example/auth/github/callback]
Wildcard matching Off [broadens allowed redirects to matching subdomains and paths when enabled; keep off for fixed callbacks; enable only if essential and you control every possible matching subdomain and path]
Device Flow Off [lets a CLI or other headless app ask the user to authorize through a code in a separate browser; keep off for this standard web callback flow; enable only when implementing device flow]
Expire user access tokens On; default [issues short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens; ongoing access needs secure token renewal; keep enabled with refresh support; disable only temporarily while updating an older client that cannot refresh]

Production values: replace the example domain with the real deployed website for your agent application. Homepage URL is its public landing page; Redirect URI is the actual backend endpoint that receives GitHub's authorization response. The callback path shown is illustrative: implement your chosen endpoint and register its URL according to GitHub's redirect URL rules. The OAuth guide website's address is not automatically your agent application's callback. These production examples were not tested; the loopback addresses above are the values validated locally.

Setting explanations: app metadata, wildcard matching and its security conditions, device flow, and token expiration and refresh. These explain choices; the local test exercised only the recorded values. Wildcards, device flow, and token refresh were not tested.

Click Register application. The live page reported Application created successfully. The saved loopback URLs were checked. Current UI supports up to 10 redirect URIs. “Private local” is the purpose of this test, not a GitHub OAuth App privacy setting: no private/public distribution toggle was observed.

Evidence: previously observed live; no registration screenshot captured. The following screenshots are official documentation, not proof of our registration.

2. Obtain the test app's secret securely

The app page showed Client ID and Generate a new client secret. Clicking secret generation required GitHub Confirm access. The user completed its verification directly in Chrome; no code entered chat. The existing generated secret was then transferred directly inside the browser-control runtime into mode-600 transient local input, without printing it or creating another secret.

Evidence: previously observed live; no credential screenshot captured. Secret UI behavior is an observation, not inferred from docs. Keep credentials out of models, chat, URLs and logs. Official secret-handling guidance.

3. Authorize with no extra scopes

In plain English

Scopes are the permissions an app asks for. This test requested no extra scopes: consent showed public-data-only access, with no private repository, email, or write permissions requested.

Human responsibility: review the consent screen and approve only intended access. In this recorded test, host automation accepted the already-authorized read-only request; the user did not personally click this consent.

App responsibility: after approval, GitHub returns a temporary authorization code to the callback. The backend validates the response before exchanging that code. You do not copy the code or token into chat.

The local client bound the exact callback above, generated random state and S256 PKCE, and opened GitHub's authorization endpoint without requesting scopes. The first live consent displayed Public data only; host automation accepted the already-authorized read-only request. No repo, organization, email, admin or write permissions were requested.

Validate returned state before exchanging the code. The current GitHub web flow requires the app secret as well as the PKCE verifier; PKCE does not remove that documented requirement. Official authorization flow.

Evidence: consent and callback observed live; no consent screenshot captured. No-scope means public read access, not anonymous access. Prior grants may carry permissions forward, so inspect actual granted scopes. Scope behavior.

4. Exchange and make one read-only API call

What our validation completed

TESTED BY VALIDATION AGENT — PASSED
This step was actually executed during our local test on October 28, 2026. The validation agent used browser automation and a local test client to exchange GitHub's temporary authorization code for an access token, then used that token for one read-only account-profile request. Both requests succeeded. No extra permissions were granted and no GitHub content was changed. Claude supplied research and plan checks; host automation executed the test. This result validates our local setup; your deployed application still needs its own test.

What your application must implement

Your deployed application still needs its own callback endpoint, state validation, secure code-to-token exchange, and permitted API request handling. The future web application has not been implemented or validated by this local experiment.

What “exchange” and “read” mean

The backend trades the temporary code for an access token—a credential used to make API requests within the granted access. This web flow also uses the app secret and the PKCE verifier.

The local test client then used that token for one authenticated read of GET /user. HTTP 200 confirmed the request worked. That read did not modify anything; the saved result records status and identity-shape checks, not account profile fields.

Who does this? the app/backend handles the code exchange and API request automatically after consent. This test used a local Python client; Claude did not directly execute the OAuth/API flow.

What this step proves: the tested application could obtain OAuth access and use it for the permitted read. The result does not establish refresh, other API operations, or production readiness. The explanation below records how we reached that result, including the initial certificate issue.

The first callback/state succeeded, but Python's default CA store failed TLS verification before the token endpoint returned HTTP. A credential-free diagnostic verified GitHub with the OS CA bundle. The client then used /etc/ssl/cert.pem while retaining certificate and hostname verification. No TLS bypass was used.

A fresh flow reused the same secret and existing consent. Callback/state validated; the fixed code-exchange endpoint returned HTTP 200 and empty granted scopes. The client sent the resulting bearer token for exactly one GET https://api.github.com/user, receiving HTTP 200. It recorded only status and identity-shape booleans, never profile fields. Official exchange and bearer use.

5. Cleanup, attribution and limits

The listener exited and its port was checked closed. Transient credential input and authorization URL file were removed. Access/refresh tokens stayed in process memory and were discarded on exit. The GitHub app, one secret and public-data grant remain; nothing was revoked, deleted or rotated.

Claude fetched official sources, rechecked the flow, and produced sanitized draft notes. Host CUA performed UI actions; the local Python client performed OAuth/API execution. Claude had no connected Chrome session and did not independently use the token. Host review corrected draft wording and attribution; unsupported plan directives in Claude's response were not executed.

Evidence File / limitation
Live API results result.json
Test client oauth_check.py
Full validation report
Earlier registration / consent Live observed; no screenshot
Approval / publishing / org access Not attempted

No human action remains for this completed check. Refresh, revocation and production deployment were not tested; timing and approval durations are unknown. A deployed web service does not inherit this host browser session: it needs its own callback and secure per-user execution path. This experiment validates local read-only OAuth, not production service readiness.

GitHub OAuth read-only end-to-end validation

Date: 2026-10-28. Status: succeeded — host-executed OAuth exchange and one authenticated API read.

Actual outcome

The existing personal-account OAuth App OAuth Guide validation completed a fresh authorization-code flow with random state and S256 PKCE. GitHub returned an access token with empty granted scopes. The temporary client used that bearer token for exactly one fixed GET https://api.github.com/user, receiving HTTP 200 and a structurally valid authenticated identity response. It emitted no profile fields or credential values.

Check Observed result
Callback received true
Returned state validated true
PKCE S256 used true
Requested OAuth scopes empty
Token-exchange HTTP status 200
Token exchange succeeded true
Granted scopes empty true
Access token expires true
Refresh token returned true
Authenticated API operation GET /user
API HTTP status 200
Response contains expected identity shape true; actual identity omitted
API OAuth-scope header empty true
Refresh behavior tested false

This was an authenticated /user request using the newly exchanged OAuth bearer token, not an unauthenticated public-profile lookup. No repository, org, email, write, or admin scopes were requested; no repositories or unrelated account data were fetched.

Actual sequence and corrections

  1. Registration was previously observed live and succeeded with loopback homepage http://127.0.0.1:8765, callback http://127.0.0.1:8765/callback, wildcard matching off, Device Flow off, and expiring-token default on. Earlier registration steps were not screenshotted.
  2. Generating the one test-app secret required GitHub Confirm access. The user completed verification directly; no code was requested or handled in chat.
  3. Revalidation found the existing generated secret. It was transferred directly inside browser-control runtime to a mode-600 transient file, never printed to tool/model output. No duplicate secret was generated.
  4. First consent showed Public data only. Callback arrived and state matched, but Python's default certificate store failed to verify GitHub before token-exchange HTTP completed. No authenticated API request occurred in that attempt.
  5. A credential-free diagnostic confirmed the trusted OS bundle /etc/ssl/cert.pem verifies GitHub. The client was changed to use that bundle while retaining TLS certificate/hostname verification. No certificate bypass was used.
  6. CUA reset interrupted credential reuse. After the user opened a neutral blank tab, control was safely reacquired and the same existing secret transferred with output suppressed. No secret rotation occurred.
  7. A fresh flow reused the previous public-data grant without requiring another consent click. Fresh callback/state validated; code exchange and the single authenticated API read both returned HTTP 200.
  8. The browser reached a query-free local completion message. The listener exited; transient credential input and authorization URL file were absent, and the local port was verified closed.

Execution and Claude attribution

Claude CLI previously fetched official GitHub docs successfully. On the retry it again completed with process exit 0, final result success, is_error: false, and successfully fetched the current authorization-flow source. Its Chrome connection returned an empty list; it did not operate Chrome or call GitHub with a token.

Host CUA performed actual browser actions; the temporary local Python client performed token exchange and authenticated read. Claude also completed a sanitized guide-note synthesis invocation with exit 0/result success. Its draft included unused plan directives and some imprecise wording; host review corrected attribution and TLS wording before saving guide.md. No draft directives were executed. This demonstrates a local agent-controlled execution path can complete OAuth and use resulting access; it does not demonstrate Claude independently controlling a browser, or a deployed website inheriting the user's host-browser session.

Client safety checks

Client: /tmp/github-oauth-validation/oauth_check.py.

The client binds only loopback, uses exact callback path, random state, S256 PKCE, no requested scopes, fixed endpoint/method allowlist, redirect refusal, rejection of missing/non-empty grant-scope evidence, verified TLS, suppressed request logging, no token/profile persistence, a bounded listener, and a query-free completion redirect. Offline self-check passed the RFC PKCE S256 vector, verifier/challenge lengths, state comparison, and loopback host check.

Sanitized result: /tmp/github-oauth-validation/result.json. First failed-attempt result is separately preserved at /tmp/github-oauth-validation/first-attempt-result.json. Neither contains secrets, tokens, codes, or profile fields.

Residual state and limits

The test OAuth App, its single generated secret, and the public-data authorization/grant remain on GitHub. No app/secret/grant was deleted, rotated, or revoked. The new access/refresh tokens existed only in the client process and were discarded when it exited; GitHub's issued credentials can remain valid server-side until expiry/revocation. No token/profile files remain locally. No listener remains.

No additional human action is required for this completed test. Refresh, revocation, organization approval, repository access, distribution, provider review, production hosting, secure multi-user credential storage and deployed-service browser access were not tested. No approval or duration estimate is claimed.
